title: NIL Ends. Your Audience Doesn’t Have To.
html:
There is a date in your future that nobody at your school will put in a slide deck. It is the day your eligibility ends.

Everything on the money side of college sport is attached to that date. The revenue-share payment is attached to it. The collective deal is attached to it. Most of your brand deals are attached to it too, because what a brand is actually buying is your visibility, and your visibility is currently being manufactured, for free, by an athletic department with a broadcast contract.

One thing is not attached to that date: the people who follow you because of who you are.

That is the whole argument. Everything below is detail.

The money is real, and it is a wage

Let us be accurate, because the numbers have got serious. Following the House settlement approved in June 2025 — around $2.8 billion in back damages plus a decade of revenue sharing — schools can distribute roughly $20.5 million among their athletes in the 2025–26 year, with the cap rising over the following decade toward the low thirties of millions. Third-party NIL continues alongside it: the College Sports Commission had cleared around $355 million of deals as of July 2026, against a third-party market widely estimated above $1 billion annually.

This is a good thing. Athletes generating billions in revenue should be paid, and now they are.

But be clear about what kind of money it is. Revenue share is compensation for participation. It is paid because you are on the roster, it stops when you are not, and its size is set by a cap you did not negotiate, in a system litigated by other people. It behaves like a wage — a very good wage, for a very short career.

A wage is not an asset. You can earn a lot of money and own nothing, and athletes have been doing exactly that for a century.

What an asset looks like

An asset produces after you stop working. For an athlete in 2026, there is really only one candidate that is available now, costs nothing to start, and does not depend on going pro: an audience with a direct relationship to you.

The reason to start during college is not sentimental. It is that your distribution is free right now and it will never be free again. Every game televised, every highlight clipped by the conference, every walk-out shot — that is audience acquisition being paid for by somebody else. The moment eligibility ends, the machine that was generating attention on your behalf switches off, and if nothing captured that attention into a relationship you control, it simply disperses.

Ask any athlete three years out of college how many people still follow them. The number is not zero. It is also, almost always, far smaller than the number of people who watched them play — because attention that is never converted into a relationship does not persist.

The trap in the obvious answer

The obvious answer is "so build a big social following". That is right in direction and incomplete in a way that matters.

A follower count on a mainstream platform is not a relationship you own. You cannot export the list. You cannot contact those people directly. You cannot take them anywhere. Reach is throttled and then sold back to you as promotion. The rate you are paid, if you are paid at all, is set by a formula you cannot see and can be changed without notice — that is not a hypothetical, it is what happened across the industry in 2017–2019, when platform policy changes wiped out monetisation for large numbers of established creators, in some cases over years-old material.

So the goal is not followers. The goal is a relationship that survives a platform changing its mind: something you can contact, something you can charge, something that moves with you.

Where we come in, stated plainly

We build one of the options, so read this as an argument rather than neutral advice.

DeHub is an open-source, decentralised social network. Three things about it are relevant to an athlete specifically:

Your posts are minted on-chain to your wallet when you publish. The ownership record is yours and does not depend on us continuing to exist. That is the difference between a deed and a tenancy.

The revenue share is published, up to 90%, rather than set by an undisclosed formula, with no follower threshold to unlock it. You can also attach watch-to-earn bounties that pay viewers in crypto for genuinely watching — useful when your content is long-form and your audience is small but intense.

Subscriptions are tradable and pay you a royalty when resold. A supporter who backed you as a sophomore can pass that subscription on, and you still earn from the resale. See tokenised subscriptions explained.

None of this requires you to leave anywhere. Keep every account you have. The point is to stop having exactly one.

Compliance, honestly

This is the part where most articles wave vaguely, so: NIL rules vary by state, by conference and by institution, disclosure requirements are real, and the House-era clearing process for third-party deals is active and being enforced. Earning money from your own content is generally NIL activity, crypto-denominated earnings raise tax questions, and none of this is legal or tax advice.

Talk to your compliance office before you monetise anything, and keep records. The build-an-audience part — posting, publishing, owning your work — is not the part that creates compliance risk. Getting paid is. Do that deliberately.

The five-year version

Picture two athletes with identical careers. Both are well-known on campus, both take NIL money, neither goes pro.

The first spent four years posting to platforms that rented them an audience. On the day eligibility ends, the department stops promoting them, the algorithm stops surfacing them, and within eighteen months the attention has gone somewhere else. They have money in the bank, which is not nothing, and no audience, which is not either.

The second did everything the first did, plus one thing: published somewhere the work was theirs and the audience could be reached directly. Same career, same money — but on the day the eligibility clock hits zero, they still have a business. Smaller than it was at peak visibility, certainly. But it is theirs, it compounds, and it does not care whether they ever play again.

The difference between those two athletes is not talent. It is about twenty minutes a week, started early, on ground they owned.

Your visibility peaks while you are eligible. Your ownership does not have to end there.

Frequently asked questions

Is posting my own content an NIL issue?

Publishing is generally not the problem; being paid is. NIL rules differ by state, conference and school, disclosure obligations are real, and the post-House clearing process applies to third-party deals. Speak to your compliance office before you monetise, and keep records of everything.

I am not a star. Is this worth it if my following is small?

Arguably more so. A small audience with a direct relationship is worth more than a large one you cannot contact, and it is far easier to build the habit at 2,000 followers than to retrofit it at 200,000. The per-piece and watch-to-earn models also work better at small scale than ad revenue does.

Does revenue sharing not solve this already?

It solves being underpaid while you are eligible, which was a genuine injustice. It does not create an asset. Revenue share stops when you leave the roster; the point of this article is the part that does not stop.

Do I need to understand crypto to use DeHub?

No. You can sign in with Google, Apple, email or SMS and a wallet is created for you in the background, with gas sponsored for non-wallet sign-ins. Payouts settle in DHB, which trades on decentralised exchanges and on Coinbase, so what you earn is liquid rather than points inside one app.

Should I stop posting on Instagram and TikTok?

No. They are where your reach is and you should keep using them. The argument is to stop depending on them exclusively — treat them as discovery and build a home base you actually own alongside.
